rv.q: You enter a fan of Celine, you leave a fan of Marla.
Titaníque on Broadway is bigger than a mere hoot.
It’s one of the many faces of resistance.
The opening of the cult hit “Titaníque”— the musical spoof of the 1997. Oscar-winning smash “Titanic” — is the latest theatrical evidence that one can be stupid and smart at the same time.

Mindelle clearly adores her subject in all of its Francophone campery and that sets the tone for a show that is impossible not to find amusing and that deftly manages to avoid reminding you even for a second that this was a disaster that killed hundreds of people.
“Titaníque” may be uneven, but at least it fits right in.
This is still a consistently very funny show, one electrified by a handful of true full-belt diva moments and unreasonably committed to its bit in a way befitting of Dion.
Titanique is still the most amusingly delightful, brilliantly performed, show biz vessel on the seven seas.
Titanique doesn’t just survive the jump to Broadway.
Now, amped up about as high as it can go with an all-star cast, Titaníque is guaranteed to deliver the most fun night you will have at the theatre this year.
Most importantly, Titanique is an absolute blast.

rv.q: It is, at least, good for a few laughs, if you are tolerant or have a buzz on.
And I'd be remiss if I did not reiterate that the cast, as well as the design elements, definitely rises above the low-brow material.
If “Titanique” gives off a distinctly amateur vibe, its goofiness is professionally honed.
As an easygoing satire of the film’s silly Rose-Jack-Cal romantic plot, Titanique succeeds at being even sillier, but at least it offers a happy ending.
But its appeal is narrow, and its comic returns diminish quickly.
Instead, I disappointedly report that Titanique—narrated by uncanny Dion lookalike Mindelle as an arch diva—is my idea of lowbrow entertainment at its just about lowest.
The entire cast is having a blast, and their infectious fun spreads generously to the audience.
Titanique has built the stage out, deeper into the audience and with steps, allowing the performers to come down to our level, racing up and down the aisles.
Titanique is a fabulous, lunatic, camp triumph on Broadway.
Titaníque earns its Broadway berth, sequins and all.
Titaníque, complete with that Frenchified accent to emphasize the final syllable, is one of the funniest musical comedies in years.
One of Titanique’s greatest strengths is not taking itself too seriously, and leaning into the idea of theatre as entertainment: funny, sexy, over dramatic, and not requiring much thought to enjoy.
What it does have going for it, is the pure entertainment factor, and a cast that is having a great time doing what they do, enjoying it just as much as the avid fans in the audience.

cn.t: Critics find this campy Céline Dion/Titanic parody hilariously unhinged and crowd-pleasing, though some worry it lost scrappy Off-Broadway charm in its Broadway transfer. Most praise the outrageous concept and performances, but a few remain unmoved by the mayhem.

sg.ra: Rows B-L are the house's actual sweet-spot band — Row A loses legroom and cranes necks because the St. James stage is raised on multiple recent productions (Sunset's LED wall, Something Rotten!'s set), while Row L is the last row before both the shallow rake AND the mezzanine overhang bite into the view Rows M+ hit the St. James's signature rake-and-overhang double-whammy — shorter patrons report 'craning around heads' and top-of-stage cutoff; a below-average experience for a 1,710-seat house

The Row D aisle-angled seats (D1/D2) are a genuine St. James unicorn — the row is set at a different angle than the rows in front so no seat sits directly ahead of you; this bypasses the flat-rake problem that defines the rest of the house 'Partial view' labeled seats in rows A-C side orchestra are heavily production-dependent — Into The Woods and Sunset (downstage-centric) work fine; Frozen's left-side set wall and Something Rotten!'s spread staging defeat them Back rows Q-S side orchestra sit directly under the mezzanine overhang — OK view of downstage action but top-of-set elements (screens, signage) cut off

Front mezzanine (Row A) is frequently called the best seat in the 1,710-seat house — Wikipedia notes the mezz 'extends over what were originally the tenth row of orchestra seats,' so you're unusually close for an upper tier, and because the orchestra's rake is so shallow, veterans repeatedly prefer Row A mezz to mid-orchestra at this specific house Row A has two specific St. James quirks that are production-sensitive — a low brass railing and an extension lighting rig on the mezz front; fine for average height but shorter patrons hit them, and Sunset Boulevard's onstage-lip blocking can make Row A worse than Row B-C

Front rows A-C side mezzanine are the house's best discount — St. James veterans (Patash: 'Gypsy, Bullets Over Broadway, A Funny Thing Happened... my favorite seats... I don't mind the side section in the least') buy them deliberately over pricier orchestra for every major musical High-seat-number side mezz (>18 in rows B-F) hits the mezzanine curvature problem — not just off-angle but the row pitches away from the stage creating sub-inch knee clearance Row B seat 18 area (where pricing typically breaks to a cheaper bracket) is a genuine value sweet spot — view is nearly identical to Row A but noticeably cheaper; confirmed across multiple productions

Rear mezz is the house's classic value trap — priced as mezzanine but the rake flattens and you're a third of the way back in a 1,710-seat house; reviewers describe needing seat boosters and sliding to the seat edge to see anything. Row Q aisle has an additional specific quirk: a corridor-exit light stays on during the show. Row J is the one exception in the rear-mezz block — it's the first row of a rear bank with a walkway in front, so no heads block the view; veterans specifically target it as the discount version of front mezz

Row A center balcony is the upper-tier's saving grace — BWW veterans split sharply (one calls it 'one of the worst balconies on Broadway', others swear by it), but the consensus lands on Row A specifically because the no-lean position, sound improvement from the extra speaker truss, and low railing make it better than rear mezz for the same price The balcony is a physical climb — 'like climbing a tower' — and is the second balcony; older patrons or anyone with mobility should not attempt at this house specifically Row A is the ONLY row that reliably clears the railing — behind Row A the rail bisects the stage; chain-reaction lean-forward effect forces everyone below to follow suit

Side balcony behind Row A combines every St. James hazard in one seat — side-angle, railing blocking downstage, second-balcony height, tight legroom, and (per multiple patrons) lottery-only sales because the house knows they're problematic Row A side balcony aisle seats (1-3 L, 2-4 R) are the one exception — sightlines avoid the railing, you're 'almost right over the front of the mezzanine,' and legroom is usable; anything behind Row A or away from the aisle is genuinely skip-tier at this house because back side-balcony also carries sound-mix issues off-axis from the speaker truss

vr.q: If you've never seen Titanique before, I don't know that there's ever been a better time.
This show has no right being this funny because it's so stupid. But it's so well done.
Not only does it combine brilliant vocal performances of great songs with hysterically funny pop culture references... it's poking fun, but there's also a real love in it as well.
A cavernous Broadway theatre is not where this type of comedy and audience interaction thrives.
